articles.title: How Notable Capital, GIC, and Baillie Gifford bet big on Anthropic before its IPO
articles.description: Three significant backers share what gave them conviction to bet billions on Anthropic.
articles.content: When Notable Capital poured roughly 10% of the U.S. portion of its $1 billion-plus fund into Anthropic’s Series E, many limited partners were perplexed by the massive bet. Claude’s maker was still trailing its biggest rival, OpenAI, and DeepSeek had released its R1 model just weeks earlier, threatening to overtake closed-source competitors. Moreover, at $61.5 billion, Anthropic’s valuation was by far the highest that the predominantly early-stage venture firm had invested at in its 25-year history. But investors at Notable, formerly known as GGV Capital before its 2024 split from its China operations, were confident in Anthropic’s future. A team that included managing partners Hans Tung and Glenn Solomon and principal Dan Cahana crunched the numbers and found that developers were increasingly favoring Claude over ChatGPT, using Claude 70% of the time, a reversal from the previous year. “We just knew that for AI, the developer is at the center because they’re the early adopters,” Tung, a co-founder of the firm, told TechCrunch. Having navigated the complexities of U.S.-China relations firsthand, Notable was also convinced that “mission-critical” work would always require U.S.-based, closed-source models, Tung said. Less than two years later, Notable’s LPs are no longer questioning the outsized investment. On Wednesday, Anthropic raised $81.3 billion in the largest IPO in history, reaching a fully diluted valuation of about $1.5 trillion before its shares began trading the next day, a paper return of roughly 15 times. Notable is, of course, not the only firm sitting on a massive paper windfall from Anthropic. Even traditional late-stage investors, who rarely see venture-scale multiples, are set for a big win. Singaporean sovereign wealth fund GIC had been researching Anthropic throughout 2024, but it didn’t make its first investment until after Chris Emanuel, head of the fund’s tech investments, met with Anthropic CFO Krishna Rao at Che Fico, an Italian restaurant in San Francisco, in early 2025. Rao helped pique Emanuel’s interest in the company by showing that model improvements were driving rising enterprise adoption. GIC then made its first investment in Anthropic’s Series F, a round announced in September 2025 at a $183 billion valuation. “Claude Code was just released then,” Emanuel told TechCrunch. “It was very early, but even then, we could see signs that it was really popular with developers.” GIC’s conviction in the AI lab was so high that the fund later led Anthropic’s Series G alongside Coatue at a $380 billion valuation, and returned as one of the co-leads for the pre-IPO round at $965 billion. Across the three rounds, GIC invested more than $4.5 billion in Anthropic, amassing a stake equal to about 1% of the company after its IPO, according to a person familiar with GIC’s financials. Lillian Li, who leads U.S. growth investments at Baillie Gifford, began studying Anthropic and speaking with its team nearly two years before first investing in the company’s Series F. Baillie Gifford invested in the Claude maker once it became clear that the company was “executing consistently” on its vision while generating strong revenue and “compelling gross margins,” Li told TechCrunch. After Baillie Gifford’s initial investment, Anthropic continued to deliver on its promises, expanding into industries such as legal services and life sciences, as well as broader applications like Cowork and cybersecurity, Li said. “It’s actually quite incredible how consistent they have been with how quickly everything’s been changing,” she added. Baillie Gifford went on to invest a total of $1.5 billion across three funding rounds, a bet that has generated substantial paper gains for the investment manager, as well as for dozens of other backers who invested at what once seemed like astronomical valuations. NYC pol sets record straight as viral ‘eyes’ video sparks looney lizard people theories: ‘Full-blown ‘Men In Black”
articles.content: See more of our coverage in your search results. A New York state politician clapped back at cold-blooded crazies who launched a conspiracy theory that he’s a reptile after a bizarre clip of his eyes circulated on social media. The reptile accusations swirled after conspiracy sleuths captured Jordan Wright, a Democratic Assemblyman for New York’s 70th District in Harlem, standing in the crowd during a City Hall press conference about a plan to shut down Rikers Island on Friday. Wright, 32, appeared to flash a small grin before blinking and rolling his eyes in the back of his head as Mayor Zohran Mamdani spoke to reporters. “This is how lizards blink … I am pretty sure there is full-blown ‘Men in Black’ aliens walking among us disguised as human beings, and they are hiding in plain sight,” one conspiracy theorist said in a video of Wright on social media. Wright scaled back the speculation in a statement to The Post, assuring that his work as a lawmaker shows he’s “obviously” human. “I have no idea what was going on in that video. I’m really not sure,” Wright admitted. “Obviously I’m a human being, and my humanity can be seen through my legislation like the $4 million for the WE ACT environmental justice center in Harlem,” he said. “I can’t speak to any reptiles or aliens.” Wright, the son of Manhattan Democratic Party chairman Keith LT Wright, championed the $4 million allocation of funds from the state’s capital projects budget for the center, which is under construction in West Harlem. The incumbent assemblyman won his reelection campaign to represent District 70 in November. The district covers Manhattanville, part of Hamilton Heights, and most of Central Harlem. Wright ran uncontested in the general election after beating democratic socialist Conrad Blackburn in the Democratic Party primary in June. During the Friday press conference, Mamdani vowed to reduce New York’s jail population by a whopping 2,500 inmates in five years and unveiled a sweeping plan to close Rikers Island by 2032. The City Council will need to approve the five-year delay, which would see the jail network shutter in 2032, when all the smaller lockups are expected to be completed. The conspiracy theory that politicians are secretly lizard people was popularized by the tinfoil-hat crowd in the 20th century, including in Robert E. Howard’s “Conan the Barbarian” stories, which feature reptilian humanoids controlling minds. The theory continues to proliferate online, including among QAnon groups.

articles.content: Lansing’s new City Hall opens to the public Monday. It’ll open a bit later than usual, at 9 a.m., to give staff a chance to do things like unpack. But the building was opened on time and on budget, before the end of the year and funded from a $40 million state appropriation. Deputy Mayor Christopher Mumby shows off of the new Lansing City Hall, 425 S. Grand. The first floor “one stop shop” area will have the city’s clerk, treasurer and assessor as well as self-service kiosks. Mike Ellis/City Pulse The public heart of the new Lansing City Hall, 425 S. Grand, will have the city’s clerk, treasurer and assessor and self-service kiosks. Mike Ellis/City Pulse City Council will meet in this room, with a capacity of about 155 with overflow space for another 35. Mike Ellis/City Pulse A peek inside the new Lansing City Hall, 425 S. Grand. Mike Ellis/City Pulse A small workstation inside the new Lansing City Hall, 425 S. Grand. Mike Ellis/City Pulse The building is designed for efficient public service, making the “one stop shop” area on the first floor, where the public goes, look like a bank or a post office with teller windows and kiosks. Mayor Andy Schor has emphasized the “one stop shop” focus throughout his role in the process. A new city hall has been a priority of mayors since at least David Hollister in the 1990s and this new city hall will retain the name of David Holliser, who died in September, just two months before the opening. Hollister was involved in some of the planning elements of the current building, including where his name will appear, said deputy mayor Christopher Mumby, who hosted City Pulse and other media in a tour of the building on Wednesday. More than 200 city workers will work in the building, IT workers began moving in recently but most workers didn’t get to move in until late last week or on Monday. Most of city buisness will be done – at least the public facing side – from the building. Bills, permits, economic development, passports, city government and more will be handled at the first floor kiosks first. There are breakout rooms, conference rooms and other spaces but most of the public will be in either the “one stop shop” area or the city council chambers. The chambers will have flexible seating that can be rearranged, but not exactly tossed around like wrestling chairs, Mumby said. About 155 people can fit in the chambers, with another 35 able to sit outside the glass doors. Parking has been a key concern for people ahead of the opening. There will be 10 spaces for the public right out front and additional street parking nearby, along with a garage. The building’s funding was secured with the help of state Sen. Sarah Anthony, a Lansing Democrat who is expected to continue in her powerful role as Senate Appropriations chair, according to incoming Senate Majority Leader Darrin Camilleri, a Trenton Democrat.

Abdul El-Sayed doubles down on ‘TrumpCare’ health plan, urging president to ‘get it done’
articles.content: Democratic senator-elect reiterates suggestion to rename Medicare for All after Trump if president allows bill to pass Michigan US senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed on Sunday doubled down on naming healthcare reform legislation after Donald Trump as long as it meant the president would not impede its passage. “If he’s open to the conversation, I am open to it, too,” El-Sayed said of Trump on Sunday. “If the president is opening to signing that bill, let’s get it done.” El-Sayed made those remarks on Sunday on NBC’s Meet the Press, where he reiterated his pledge to pursue a single-payer, national healthcare program after the Democrat became the first Muslim person elected to the US Senate during the midterms earlier in November. Trump’s Republican party is going to lose control of Congress for the second half of his second presidency. But the president has made clear his intention to wield his legislative veto powers whenever he sees fit. Appearing on Sunday’s Meet the Press, El-Sayed said he would not mind Medicare for All – a big part of his campaign platform – being named “TrumpCare” as long as such a program came into existence. “I care that the people of this country finally have the unmet promise of guaranteed healthcare in this country. And if the president is serious about leaving a lasting legacy, there is nothing better than the ultimate Trump card,” El-Sayed said to Meet the Press host Kristen Welker, making a double entendre for a term that – when the T is lowercase – also refers to a card that beats out others in card games. El-Sayed told Welker that such a Trump card would be in effect “from the moment [people] are born to the moment that they pass away – that guarantees them the healthcare that has been so elusive in this country without premiums, co-pays and deductibles”. The senator-elect’s comments come after he previously suggested to CNN that he is not above stroking Trump’s prodigious ego to get legislation passed – including by naming Medicare for All “TrumpCare”. He also previously wrote on social media, alongside images of a gold health insurance card with “TrumpCare” inscribed on it: “Donald, this is on the table. Guarantee healthcare for every American, from cradle to grave.” Trump seemingly responded to El-Sayed’s post by reposting a screenshot of the senator-elect’s tweet. The president has not formally responded to the push to create universal healthcare. Trump has spent much of his second presidency trying to get as much as possible named after him – from institutions, physical buildings and currency. El-Sayed also said that he supports healthcare reform proposed by Bernie Sanders, the progressive US senator. Sanders’ proposal would create a single-payer system in which the federal government insures everybody, financed by an increase in taxes, while eliminating private insurance. But El-Sayed said he is not focused on eliminating private insurance as an option, which Sanders aims to eliminate by having everything primary and preventive services to hospital stays covered under his proposed plan. Out-of-pocket costs on deductibles and co-pays – staples of the rapacious private insurance industry to which most Americans must resort – would also be eliminated under Sanders’ plan. El-Sayed said he wants to “provide you basic public health insurance no matter who you are in this country” while being open to the idea of not taking alternative options away. The senator-elect said he has a meeting on the books with JD Vance. El-Sayed would not share the agenda of the meeting, but he confirmed that the vice-president’s chief of staff contacted him after his election victory.

Jared Goff throws 2 TDs, Jahmyr Gibbs runs for 2 more and Lions beat Bucs 31-21 for 6th straight win
articles.content: DETROIT (AP) — The Detroit Lions are finding their groove, leaning on a balanced attack offensively and a steadily improving defense that hasn’t been hurt by the losses of Aidan Hutchinson and Jack Campbell. Jared Goff threw two touchdown passes through three quarters and Jahmyr Gibbs ran for two scores in the fourth, helping Detroit pull away and beat the Tampa Bay Buccaneers 31-21 on Sunday. “We’re continuing to climb and it’s the right time,” coach Dan Campbell said. The Lions (8-2) have won six straight, setting up a pivotal NFC North game against the Chicago Bears (8-2) in a matchup of first-place teams on Thanksgiving to kick off the NFL’s tripleheader on the holiday. “We’re the first show and it’s exciting,” Campbell said. “It’s one of the reasons you do it — and love it.” Tampa Bay (3-7) has dropped two straight to fall to four games under .500, but that doesn’t doom its chances to win the NFC South. “We’re past the mulligan stage of the season, so we can’t keep shooting ourselves in the foot,” coach Todd Bowles said. Detroit’s defense sealed the win by sacking Baker Mayfield on two straight snaps and forcing the Bucs to turn it over on downs at their 34 with 3:16 remaining. The Lions have held four straight teams to 275 or fewer total yards for the first time since 1976. “That’s been the biggest growth for us,” Campbell said. “The improvement we’ve had in that group even after losing guys, that’s the sign of a championship team.” Goff was 20 of 28 for 279 yards, throwing a 14-yard pass in the end zone to Amon-Ra St. Brown in the first quarter and a 57-yard touchdown pass to Jameson Williams in the third quarter. A week after Hutchinson had a season-ending knee injury, celebrating a sack, Williams flipped into the end zone on his score. Detroit’s veteran quarterback, who isn’t known for his mobility, was nimble enough on his feet to have a season-high, 10-yard scramble to convert a third down for one of his three runs that picked up first downs and did two spin moves in the pocket to avoid a sack before completing a pass. Gibbs ran for 98 yards against a team that was giving up an NFL-low 79 yards rushing per game and turned a three-point lead into a 17-point cushion with short touchdown runs in the final quarter. The Bucs were averaging a league-high 163.9 yards rushing, but were held to 120 yards on the ground. Bucky Irving ran for just 68 yards on 18 carries and his 1-yard touchdown run late in the third made it 17-14 in a game Tampa Bay never led. “They did a better job with what they do best than we did with what we do best,” Bowles said. Mayfield, playing with an injured foot and right thumb, was 20 of 33 for 187 yards with a season-high two touchdown passes on 23 and 4 yards to rookie receiver Ted Hurst. “We made some plays, but we didn’t quite make enough,” Mayfield said. “That’s frustrating because we can do all of this in practice, but we haven’t been able to translate that to Sundays yet.” Key takeaways from Lions’ 31-21 victory against Buccaneers Lions edge rusher Ahmed Hassanein became the first Egyptian to play in an NFL game, making his debut in the league after Detroit drafted the former Boise State star in the sixth round in 2025. For the pregame coin toss, Tampa Bay sent five former Lions to midfield: Alex Anzalone, Al-Quadin Muhammad, A’Shawn Robinson, Miles Killebrew and Ifeatu Melifonwu. Each time Anzalone made a tackle, the crowd booed even though the veteran linebacker wanted to return for a sixth season in Detroit before he signed a $17 million, two-year deal with the Bucs in March. CB Jacob Parrish (back) and DL Elijah Simmons (concussion) were injured during the game. Lions: CBs D.J. Reed (hip) and Ennis Rakestraw (shoulder) were inactive.

articles.title: ‘You Can See Everything’ has made more than $100M worldwide
articles.description: The new Elizabeth Holmes documentary is just beginning to roll out internationally.
articles.content: “You Can See Everything,” Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s documentary about Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes, reached an impressive box office milestone this weekend, becoming one of the few documentaries to make more than $100 million worldwide. Variety reports that almost all of the film’s $102.4 million box office has come from U.S. audiences, from whom it has grossed $93.4 million so far. “You Can See Everything” will be opening in many more countries over the next few months — starting with Mexico, Brazil, and Argentina on November 25 and 26 — so its box office total could end up significantly higher. And while the documentary was already an undeniable commercial success for indie studio A24 (especially with a reported budget of $7 million), it could now surpass the records set by the highest-grossing documentaries of all time — “March of the Penguins” ($127 million globally) and “Fahrenheit 9/11” ($222 million globally). articles.title: The best apps to make new friends right now
articles.description: We've compiled a list of friendship apps, from friend discovery platforms like BFF to event-focused ones like Timeleft.
articles.content: In recent years, people have been increasingly looking for new ways to form platonic connections, as loneliness and social isolation have become more prevalent. In 2023, the U.S. Surgeon General went so far as to label this issue a public health crisis. Remote workers, who miss the everyday interactions found in an office, and younger individuals eager to create their adult social circles based on shared interests and hobbies, are among those seeking meaningful friendships. Thanks to online dating apps, the stigma associated with finding connections online has largely faded away. This has welcomed a new wave of apps focused on fostering friendships and building local communities. According to estimates from Appfigures, over a dozen local-focused friendship apps have collectively generated approximately $16 million in consumer spending in the U.S. so far this year. Some notable examples include Timeleft, Meet5, and Bumble’s BFF. Additionally, these apps have garnered approximately 4.3 million downloads thus far in 2025. The apps aim to provide a less awkward solution than, for instance, approaching a stranger at the gym or local café and trying to strike up a conversation. These platforms clearly indicate that everyone using the app is looking for the same thing — friendship, not romance — making it much less intimidating to initiate conversations. From major players like Meetup to newer ones like 222, there are plenty of apps that cater to the growing demand for meaningful friendships. We’ve compiled a list of them for you to try out. The app 222 is an iOS-only social events platform that facilitates in-person meetups by pairing a group of strangers based on their personality test results. The app sends invitations to nearby public social events, such as wine bars and comedy clubs. There is then a vetting process, and selected participants are notified on the day of the event. A bonus for those who feel socially anxious: You’re allowed to bring a plus-one. The service charges a $22.22 curation fee or a monthly subscription for the same price. Dating giant Bumble is among the more established players to enter the friendship space, launching its friend-finding feature in 2016, which then spun out into a stand-alone app in 2023. The friend-making app has recently undergone a significant redesign, with an increased emphasis on facilitating group meetups, catering to users’ desires to grow their social circles. BFF is available for free download on iOS and Android devices. Clyx is another emerging app in the group-based social networking landscape, with a strong focus on discovering local events. The social platform helps users find community events by integrating data from platforms like Ticketmaster and TikTok. Additionally, Clyx allows users to upload their contact lists, helping them see which events their friends plan to attend. The app also includes a feature that recommends other users to connect with at these events. As of now, Clyx operates exclusively in two cities: Miami and London. However, it has plans to expand to additional areas in the near future, with New York City and São Paulo at the top of the list. The app is available on the App Store and Google Play Store. Crowdier is a new group social app that lets friend groups connect with others. Users can create a group of 2-5 friends and browse other groups to arrange hangouts in person. To initiate a match, users can “Wave” at groups they like, and if those groups wave back, they can plan in a shared chat. A match requires the majority of both groups to agree. For example, 2 people in a 4-person group needs to say yes. The app is available for free on iOS and Android devices. Les Amís is a friendship app tailored for women, transgender, and LGBTQ+ individuals that leverages AI to match users based on similar interests and encourages participation in local events, such as pottery classes, book clubs, and wine tastings. Matches are made every Monday, allowing users to chat and plan meetups later in the week. Available on iOS and Android, Les Amís serves cities across Europe, including Amsterdam, Barcelona, Berlin, Madrid, Paris, and Stockholm. In the U.S., the app is available in Austin and New York, with plans to expand to Boston, Miami, and Los Angeles. The app uses a paid membership model that varies by city, with fees of $70 in New York and €55 in Amsterdam. The local event-discovery platform has been around since 2002, helping millions of users connect with others who share similar interests. Users can RSVP to events; join groups that cater to a variety of hobbies, professions, or social causes; and create their own groups and events. They can also chat with group members and post updates and photos from gatherings. This European community-building app recently launched in the U.S., targeting users over 40 who want to meet new people in their area and participate in group activities such as picnics, concerts, and hiking. Notably, in a short time, there have been around 777,000 U.S. downloads so far across the App Store and Google Play Store, according to Appfigures estimates. Pie is another one of the newer social apps on the market. It features an AI-driven quiz designed to predict which users are most likely to be compatible with each other. Each person who RSVPs to a Pie event takes a brief personality assessment, and the algorithm organizes attendees into groups of six, who are then added to a group chat within the Pie app, allowing them to interact with each other before the event. Currently, the app is only available in Austin, Chicago, and San Francisco. Users can download Pie from the App Store and Google Play Store. Timeleft is a relatively new platform that helps you organize weekly dinner dates with groups of strangers. The app uses a special algorithm to match you with others, taking into account your age, gender, and personality. Users are matched with four other people, but they only learn minor details about them the night before, including their occupations and zodiac signs. Dinners take place at a selected restaurant on Wednesday evenings at 7:00 p.m. To help everyone break the ice, the app offers a game with conversation starters. After dinner, there is an after-party at a local bar. Users can book dinners online or through the app. In terms of pricing, it varies depending on the country and restaurant. Users pay for a ticket up front and are responsible for covering their own dinner and drinks. Washed Up is a social event discovery app that launched in early 2026, designed for people in the Los Angeles area who want an easier way to find things to do and meet new people. The app helps users discover local events, such as concerts, trivia nights, and comedy shows, while also giving them a built-in way to connect with others who plan to attend. Instead of going to events alone, users can create or join “plans,” which are small group meetups tied to specific events. Users can browse these plans and request to join, chat with the group, and add new friends, making it easier to show up to events with people rather than by themselves. It’s available to download on the App Store. Wyzr Friends is an activity-based friendship app designed for adults 40 and older, catering to empty nesters, those who are divorced, and other users seeking to connect with like-minded individuals. Users can thumbs up or down potential friends and arrange in-person activities based on shared interests, such as going to the movies or hiking. It’s available on iOS and Android devices in the U.S., Canada, Australia, Ireland, the Philippines, Singapore, and Mexico. Mmotion is a newly launched friendship app that blends location tracking with social discovery to help users connect with people nearby and explore new bars and restaurants in their area. Upon joining, users can participate in interest-based groups — such as hiking, basketball, or art — view a map of active users, and send messages to those nearby. The app also highlights new places on the map, making it easy to find a restaurant or venue to try. Mmotion is currently only available to users in New York City on iOS and Android devices. Users must first submit an application to be considered. Launched in March 2026, Synchrony is a new social app tailored for neurodivergent adults. Founded by a mother of a son on the autism spectrum, it aims to create a supportive community through features like interest-based matching and two-step identity verification. This ensures that users engage safely, as both a user and a trusted person must verify personal details and a photo ID during registration. A standout feature is Jesse, an optional AI communication tool that assists users in navigating conversations. The AI provides editable prompts to help express thoughts, clarifies conversations, and offers boundary-setting suggestions. While the incorporation of AI may raise concerns, there are guardrails built into Jesse, such as avoiding medical advice. Users must pay a monthly subscription of $44.99 after a 30-day free trial. articles.description: Russian attack near Ukraine’s capital strikes apartment building, killing 3 and burying others AP News Boy and elderly survivor pulled from rubble after Russian attack near Kyiv Reuters At least 15 killed in Ukraine’s Kyiv region as Russia intensifies attacks Al Jazeera Child rescued alive from under the rubble in Dymer Українська правда Ukraine war briefing: Race to find survivors after Russian attack on apartment b
articles.content: KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — A Russian attack struck an apartment building in a village near Ukraine’s capital on Sunday, killing at least three people and wounding four others, authorities said. Nearly a dozen people were feared buried beneath the rubble. The morning strike destroyed the five-story building in Dymer, north of Kyiv. Rescuers evacuated nine people, including a child, while another child was hospitalized with injuries. Search and rescue teams worked to find possible survivors, with Ukraine’s State Emergency Service reporting earlier Sunday that 11 were still believed to be trapped. “When (the explosion came), I literally flipped over in bed,” said Mykola Osadnyi, a relative of some of the missing who lived nearby. “My father-in-law … was screaming, ‘Save me, I’m burning!’” he said. Another resident, Olena Kharkavliuk, said her daughter’s classmate and her mother were among those buried in the debris. Meanwhile, a rare air alert sounded in Kaliningrad, a Russian exclave near Poland and Lithuania, according to the local governor, as claims circulated online of drone activity near a major naval base there. The alert late Saturday in Kaliningrad came hours after a drone strike in the Gulf of Finland set fire to a Russian cargo ship bound for the region, which is a key base for Russia’s Baltic Fleet. Finnish emergency services were still working to extinguish the blaze on Sunday. Photos and video posted online show drone activity around the city of Baltiysk, where much of the fleet is stationed. But The Associated Press couldn’t immediately verify the authenticity of the images. According to local media, air raid sirens were heard in Kaliningrad for the first time since Russia’s all-out invasion of Ukraine on Feb. 24, 2022. The Kaliningrad governor, Alexei Besprozvannykh, said that “a suspicious object coming from the direction of Lithuania” triggered the alert in the Nemansky district near the Lithuanian border, about 170 kilometers (105 miles) northeast of Baltiysk. On Russian Telegram channels, posts by users saying they were Baltiysk residents described air defenses working during the night. They featured photos and videos of bright streaks against the night sky, with crackling sounds heard in the background. Kaliningrad authorities on Sunday denounced as fake a photo purportedly taken in Baltiysk that showed clouds of smoke rising into the night sky and an orange haze glowing on the horizon. As of Sunday morning, Russian authorities had reported no casualties or damage in Kaliningrad. Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys wrote on X that Lithuania “categorically rejects false claims” regarding the country’s involvement in a drone attack against the region. “The Republic of Lithuania has never authorized the use of its airspace for attacks against targets in the Russian Federation, including in the present case.” Lithuania’s authorities also said they hadn’t recorded any drones or similar objects flying through the country’s airspace the previous night. Meanwhile, firefighting operations aboard the Russian Sparta II cargo ship were still underway Sunday afternoon in rough weather, Finnish authorities told a news conference. The contents of the ship’s cargo remained unknown, they added. Finnish emergency teams had not entered the ship and were trying to extinguish the blaze from the outside, the officials said. The Sparta II drifted into Finland’s territorial waters after being struck by drones, the Finnish Border Guard said. A Border Guard representative told Finnish broadcaster Yle that the crew had been transferred to a Russian rescue ship. Once the fire has been extinguished, a Russian team would move the vessel out of Finland’s waters, the official said. Both Helsinki and Moscow have suggested that the drones that struck the ship were Ukrainian. Ukrainian officials did not comment. “The question of whether the ship and its cargo should be seized has been considered,” Jukka-Pekka Lumilahti, director of maritime operations at the Finnish Border Guard, said, according to Yle. “From a rescue perspective, bringing the ship to a Finnish port is extremely risky.” Also on Sunday, one civilian died and three others were injured after Russian forces hit a grocery store in Vyshneve, a western suburb of Kyiv, according to the head of the regional military administration. In Russia’s Bryansk region near the Ukrainian border, a drone attacked a civilian vehicle on Sunday and killed its driver, according to local Gov. Egor Kovalchuk. Attacks on the Russia-occupied Luhansk region in eastern Ukraine killed a cyclist and wounded three other people, Kremlin-installed local leader Leonid Pasechnik said. Ukrainian air defenses shot down or suppressed 161 of the 186 Russian drones launched overnight, including 56 jet-powered drones, according to Ukraine’s air force. Russia’s Defense Ministry on Sunday said that its forces shot down or suppressed 170 Ukrainian drones during the night — including over Russian regions, the occupied Crimean Peninsula and the Black and Azov Seas. It didn’t say how many were launched. Follow the AP’s coverage of the war in Ukraine at https://apnews.com/hub/russia-ukraine

articles.content: A coordinated rescue effort involving the Oakland County Sheriff’s Office Search and Rescue Team (SSRT), Independence Township firefighters and Byers towing company resulted in the successful extrication of an elderly Fenton man from his submerged vehicle Saturday evening in downtown Clarkston. The sheriff’s office said the incident took place about 8 p.m. on Saturday, Nov. 21 as deputies and the Independence Township Fire Department responded to the area of West Washington and North Main streets following reports of a vehicle that had entered the Mill Pond with a driver trapped inside. According to investigators, the driver of a 2026 Toyota Grand Highlander became stuck near a tree after leaving a nearby parking lot. Witnesses reported seeing the driver attempting to free the vehicle before it entered the pond. After the man was removed from the vehicle, lifesaving measures were immediately initiated, and he was transported to McLaren Oakland Hospital, where he is listed in critical condition. “This incident demonstrates the extraordinary level of teamwork, professionalism and coordination among our emergency response partners,” Sheriff Michael J. Bouchard said. “Independence Township firefighters, our Search and Rescue Team and personnel from Byers Wrecker Service worked seamlessly under extremely challenging circumstances to give this man the best possible chance of survival.” The incident also prompted the activation of specialized dive teams from the Southeast Michigan Dive Group, including personnel from the Genesee, Macomb and Clinton County sheriff’s offices and the fire units from Chesterfield Township and Shelby Township in Macomb County. The vehicle was subsequently recovered and impounded. Investigators believe alcohol may have been a contributing factor in the crash. The circumstances surrounding the incident remain under investigation by the Oakland County Sheriff’s Office.

articles.content: Powerful living: The net-zero energy community Veridian at County Farm will host Michigan’s first residential virtual power plant with battery manufacturer Sonnen USA. (Veridian at County Farm) Mitch Hall and his wife, Lori, live in one of the most sustainable communities in the U.S. Their town house is among a few dozen residences constructed so far at Veridian at County Farm, a fossil-fuel-free, net-zero-energy development in Ann Arbor, Michigan. Homes here make about as much solar energy as they consume, with the help of batteries that save solar power for use in the evenings. Now, the couple is eager to share the benefits of their clean energy infrastructure with the wider grid. In the coming weeks, Veridian households can enroll in Michigan’s first residential pilot of a virtual power plant; Detroit-based utility DTE Energy will then be able to remotely control the network of residents’ home batteries to inject their stored solar power onto the grid when operators need it most. “This pilot is an opportunity to test an approach that could ultimately provide a lower-cost way to meet growing energy needs and strengthen reliability,” Joi Harris, president and chief executive officer of DTE Energy, said in a statement. VPPs can smooth out demand peaks, reducing the utility’s need to invest in grid-infrastructure upgrades and generate kilowatt-hours with expensive fossil-fuel peaker plants, both of which would pile costs on consumers. The initiative ​“should work well for the residents, too,” Hall said. ​“DTE will pay us a little bit to be part of this project.” Because the utility will pull battery power automatically when the grid is strained and electricity prices are likely to be highest, ​“a neat part about the virtual power plant is you don’t have to spend a lot of time learning and trying to optimize,” he noted. ​“DTE will manage that battery for you.” (DTE did not respond to Canary Media’s request for exact figures on how much it would compensate customers in time for publication.) VPPs have existed for years but have been slow to gain widespread traction because of a host of factors. Utilities often haven’t been incentivized to embrace the approach, while home solar and batteries remain too expensive for many households in the U.S. But as electrification and the data center rush spur unprecedented demand, VPPs are taking off as a fast way to get power on the grid. Earlier this month, the Brattle Group estimated that 524 gigawatts of distributed energy resources harnessed in VPPs could save households on average $122 per year by 2050. Currently, ​“there’s immense untapped capacity,” said Kevin Brehm, manager in the carbon-free electricity practice at clean energy think tank RMI. Matt Grocoff, the founder of Thrive Collaborative, started to consider a VPP pilot at Veridian in 2019. He wanted the neighborhood to mimic an ecosystem — a resilient web of relationships in which individual organisms do more than just extract resources. For example, a tree in a forest turns sunlight into nutrients and shares them symbiotically with a vast, interconnected underground web of fungi. Likewise, with a VPP, each Veridian home ​“can be producing energy that it needs and mutually beneficially sharing it across a network of energy rather than a linear grid that flows in only one direction,” Grocoff said. DTE expects nearly 100 battery-equipped Veridian homes to ultimately participate in the pilot. So far, 44 market-rate homes with solar and batteries have been built, out of 120 planned, as have 50 affordable housing units that don’t have batteries yet, according to Thrive Collaborative. Battery manufacturer Sonnen USA, maker of the home storage systems installed at Veridian, is helping DTE operate the pilot using Sonnen’s proprietary software. “Veridian is a test bed,” said Geoff Ferrell, executive vice president of Sonnen USA’s VPP business unit. The initiative, which is expected to be able to deliver up to about 300 kilowatts for three hours, will give DTE a clearer picture of how much power the home battery fleet can actually generate and when, providing ​“a really great basis” for a scaled-up program, he noted. Ferrell points to another Sonnen-facilitated VPP that also sprang up as a humble pilot project, but rapidly mushroomed into a full-scale program because of early positive results. That initiative started in 2017 with a new apartment building topped with solar, Soleil Lofts outside Salt Lake City. Sonnen hadn’t even finished installing batteries in each of the development’s 600 units when the utility Rocky Mountain Power and the state utility commission decided that the initial data was promising enough to merit extending the program to every residential customer in the utility’s territory, Ferrell said. Today, about 7,900 homes and businesses participate in the program, now called Wattsmart Battery, in Utah, Wyoming, and Idaho. Given the success of that VPP and many others, Brehm would like to see more utilities go full throttle at the outset. “Do you need another pilot?” he asked, noting that numerous VPP programs exist for utilities to model their own programs after. But for utilities that do approach VPPs with caution, Rocky Mountain Power’s pilot is a good model, according to Brehm. The utility’s employees were able to rapidly understand how the residential battery fleet worked and how to deploy it, he said, ​“so that they could integrate these batteries into their operations initially, and subsequently [into their resource-capacity] planning.” He’d like to see DTE do the same. The VPP pilot at Veridian is already starting to inspire developers and utilities outside Michigan, including the development Peace Hill in Townsend, Washington, said Grocoff of Thrive Collaborative. “We’re getting calls from all over the country,” Grocoff said. ​“It’s really exciting.”

Can a TV be too large? An investigation
articles.description: Can a TV be too large? This writer's recent upgrade to a 65-inch OLED came with some unexpected challenges.
articles.content: For the past couple of years, I’ve wanted to upgrade my home entertainment situation from the humble trappings of my long sufficient 55-inch TCL smart TV to the model much coveted by cinephiles the world over: the OLED. The organic light-emitting diode is a specific monitor technology that has really changed the TV industry. Unlike an LED TV, which creates images by shining a backlight through a panel of pixels, OLEDs leverage millions of self-lighting pixels, which provides significantly better pixel control, and can generate a much more nuanced image with deeply vibrant colors and a more intense light and shadows. They are also significantly more expensive, which is one reason that I’ve held off on investing in one for years. However, this year I couldn’t wait any longer. I finally sprang for an upgrade and, since I was already upgrading on image quality, I decided to upgrade the size, too: I bought a 65-inch LG evo C4, which is the company’s mid-range unit released in 2024. At first, the experience was amazing. The television rendered colors and shadows wonderfully and, seeing as one of the goals with this purchase was to indulge my physical media habit, I began running through my collection of 4K Blu-ray discs with the madcap energy of a true fanatic. However, things took a bit of an unexpected turn when, midway through “McCabe and Mrs. Miller,” I was suddenly overcome by a wave of nausea. I’m not particularly sensitive to motion sickness, but this sensation — which made it feel vaguely like I was going to hurl — persisted for several hours after it initially began. It was then replaced by a small tension headache. I discovered that this is actually a somewhat common experience for new OLED adopters. Indeed, Reddit is rife with posts from new television owners who claim they feel like their big new toy is breaking their brain. “I got the tv yesterday and still feel sick today,” one Redditor, who said they had recently purchased an LG C2, wrote. “Feel light headed and nauseous a day later. Thinking about taking it back. Is this normal? I’m scared to turn the thing on lol.” Others blamed the sheer size of the screen. One guy, who bought an 85-inch TLC, claimed it had led his wife to the conclusion that “it’s too big and say that she feels sick watching. Is that a thing that a screen can be too big?” There doesn’t seem to be a consensus on why this happens. Many Redditors blame certain motion-smoothing settings. However, my TV did not come with those settings enabled. Others blamed viewers for sitting too close to the screen — yet I was sitting a solid nine feet away, which is well within the recommended range for a 65-inch screen. Finally, others have argued that the screen brightness could be agitating users’ eyes. I dialed down the brightness on mine to around 50 percent, although I had doubts as to whether this actually had anything to do with the feelings I was having. In considering my nausea, one theory that sprang to mind was that it might just be my eyes’ inexperience with viewing such a big screen. The TV was so large that it often felt like my eye had to trace different parts of the screen to take in the whole picture and, if the scene involved significant motion (most movie scenes do, after all), it conjured the sensation of trying to stare too intently at something out the window of a moving car. After a few days, however, my eyes finally adjusted. The nausea was gone. All that remained was an immense and beautiful home viewing experience that made every previous viewing experience pale by comparison. Initial physiological reactions aside, the size of the 65-inch screen (and whether your living space actually has room for it) is still something that needs to be considered carefully by potential buyers. I recently moved into a place with a slightly bigger living room, which has given me the flexibility to install a bigger device. At my old apartment, however, this size of TV would have definitely felt like it was devouring the space. Another slight frustration is that the C4 does not come with any detailed installation instructions. The screen (which is so wide it’s difficult to move without another person there to help you) comes detached from its base, and the user is just sort of expected to figure out how to effectively move and put together the two pieces. A quick YouTube video is all that is necessary to understand this process, but you have to be careful when moving and assembling the pieces so as not to scratch or damage the screen. Once the whole thing is set up and assembled, the OLED is a truly beautiful thing to behold. The customization that’s possible, including advanced brightness and color control — and things like “Filmmaker Mode” (which claims to adjust each movie’s color and frame rate settings to those intended by the director) — make the user experience really powerful. To sum up: The evo C4 is a really spectacular piece of equipment that has a lot to offer the avid home entertainment viewer — although there may be a bit of a learning curve before it makes your cinema dreams come true. articles.title: Jaafar leads Detroit Catholic Central football back to state final
articles.content: Ryan Jaafar might be due for a ratings bump of his own. Detroit Catholic Central senior Gideon Gash, a Texas Tech commit who picked up a fifth star this week, missed his second straight game because of an injury. But Jaafar was available for the Division 1 state semifinal, and, boy, did he give the recruiting sites something to consider. The senior running back came in with 1,182 rushing yards and 14 touchdowns. He added 164 yards on 26 carries and ran for three more TDs to help defending state champion Catholic Central (12-1) beat previously unbeaten East Kentwood 31-17 on Saturday, Nov. 21, at Jackson. Catholic Central won the same matchup 46-6 last year. This time, East Kentwood got the ball back down seven with 4:05 left, and Jaafar couldn’t put it away until punching in a 2-yard TD run with 1:37 to go. “Ryan Jaafar’s just a dog, man,” Catholic Central coach Justin Cessante said. “He just runs with a lot of grit.” Catholic Central will defend its title against unbeaten Romeo, which upset Detroit Cass Tech in its semifinal, at 7 p.m. Nov. 28 at Ford Field. It’ll be Catholic Central’s 19th state final appearance, giving it a chance to win back-to-back titles for the first time since its 2001-03 three-peat. The teams split their two previous playoff meetings. Romeo won 40-29 in the 2015 regional on its way to its first and only state title, and Catholic Central won 17-0 in the semifinal the next year. Cessante expects another physical game against a team that, like his own, takes pride in running downhill and stopping the run. Luke Jadan’s first-quarter interception set up Jaafar’s 21-yard TD on the next snap. JJ Chevalier blocked a punt and recovered it in the end zone to make it 14-0. Jaafar broke a run of more than 50 yards to set up Ty Goddard’s 17-yard field goal on the final play of the half, giving Catholic Central a 17-0 lead. East Kentwood answered with a 69-yard TD pass from Colin O’Connor to Donovan Rubens and a 47-yard field goal from Jayden Garcia to pull within seven. But Jaafar broke a 44-yard TD run shortly afterward. O’Connor found Steph Jones for a 28-yard TD to make it 24-17 in the fourth. East Kentwood got the ball back, but Josiah Neal hit O’Connor as he threw. Aidan Kersey jumped the route and returned the interception to the 10 to set up Jaafar’s third TD. Cessante credited his veteran offensive line for giving Jaafar room to work. “There’s a synergy between him and our line,” Cessante said. “He found some holes, ran with his eyes.” Detroit Catholic Central (12-1) vs. Romeo (13-0), 7 Saturday, Nov. 28 Muskegon Mona Shores (12-1) vs. Orchard Lake St. Mary’s (11-3), 7 p.m., Friday Nov. 27 Harper Woods (12-2) vs. Zeeland West (12-2), 12:30 p.m., Saturday Nov. 28 Grand Rapids Kenowa Hills (13-0) vs. Dearborn Divine Child (12-1), 12:30 p.m., Friday Nov. 27 Grand Rapids West Catholic (12-2) vs. Frankenmuth (13-1), 4 p.m., Saturday Nov. 28 Almont (14-0) vs. Jackson Lumen Christi (12-2), 4 p.m., Friday Nov. 27 Ithaca (12-1) vs. Ottawa Lake Whiteford (12-2), 9:30 a.m., Saturday Nov. 28 Hudson (12-1) vs. Beal City (13-0), 9:30 a.m., Friday Nov. 27 We may earn a commission when you buy through links on this page. articles.content: Voters wait in line on Nov. 3, 2026, at Bethlehem Lutheran Church in Lansing, Mich., one of several local polling places in Ingham County. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance) Stories From The States is a weekly podcast from States Newsroom that explores, through personal stories, how people and communities across America are being affected by government decisions. Listen now wherever you get your podcasts. There’s renewed interest in shifting to a national popular vote in presidential elections after Democrats’ major midterm victories. Presidents are chosen by the Electoral College, through which states decide how to award their share of 538 electors. Most states use a winner-take-all method that awards all of their electors to one candidate, even in tight races. Five of the nation’s 47 presidents took office without winning a majority of votes nationally. The National Popular Vote Interstate Compact has advocated for reform since 2006. The compact is an agreement among participating states and the District of Columbia to award all of their Electoral College votes to the presidential candidate who wins the overall national popular vote. The compact does not abolish the Electoral College, and would only take effect once states with at least 270 electoral votes sign on. Eighteen states and the District of Columbia have joined the compact, but more states could opt in soon to get to that majority. With Democrats holding “trifectas” — unified control of the governor’s office and both legislative chambers — in 22 states next year, the possibility is high. In Episode 55, Christopher Pearson, secretary of the advocacy group National Popular Vote, joins the podcast. He’ll address some misconceptions about the proposal, and why he thinks a popular vote for president could bolster voter turnout and make every vote equal. You’ll also get a weekly news wrap-up from Evening Wrap newsletter writer Danielle Gaines and Daybreak newsletter writer Madyson Fitzgerald. They’ve got you covered with the latest on: measles in the states, infant and maternal mortality and data center moratoriums. Episode produced and edited by Mallory Cheng. articles.title: GLP-1 drugs could have a surprisingly large environmental payoff
articles.description: GLP-1 drugs could cut food demand enough to free farmland larger than Italy.
articles.content: GLP-1 weight-loss medicines such as Ozempic and Wegovy could affect much more than the waistlines of the people who take them. If widely used, our new research suggests these appetite-suppressing medicines could transform the global food system and free up vast areas of agricultural land. The global food system is ultimately driven by demand. If people eat less, producers respond, affecting production, prices, trade, and how much land is needed. We used a powerful computer simulation to explore scenarios ranging from GLP-1 use concentrated in high-income countries to widespread global access. With widespread use of these medicines among adults living with obesity, we estimate that reduced calorie intake could prevent up to 6.6 million deaths each year by 2050, while freeing up as much as 32 million hectares of agricultural land—an area slightly larger than Italy—for other uses.Read full article Comments

articles.title: Midterm wins, near-misses could signal political change in the Deep South
articles.description: The midterms are over but Tennessee state Rep. Justin Pearson is back on the road, visiting churches and community centers across the congressional district he narrowly lost. He wants to thank voters who supported him. And he’s determined not to lose the connections he built during a long-shot campaign that has come to exemplify Democrats’ […]
articles.content: Tennessee Democratic state Rep. Justin Pearson turns to his wife, Oceana Pearson, during his election night party in Memphis. Pearson narrowly lost his race for Congress, and his defeat — and Democratic optimism — is part of a pattern that repeated across the Deep South up and down the midterm ballot. (Photo by Brad Vest for Tennessee Lookout)The midterms are over but Tennessee state Rep. Justin Pearson is back on the road, visiting churches and community centers across the congressional district he narrowly lost. He wants to thank voters who supported him. And he’s determined not to lose the connections he built during a long-shot campaign that has come to exemplify Democrats’ growing ambitions across the Republican-controlled South. He came closer than most anyone expected to winning. Pearson’s Republican legislative colleagues redrew the U.S. House district earlier this year to break up a longtime Democratic stronghold around the majority-Black city of Memphis, diluting it with Republican-heavy areas to net the state an additional GOP seat in Congress. And it worked. Barely. Pearson lost to Republican Brent Taylor by about 1 percentage point in the newly drawn district, which the nonpartisan Cook Political Report said President Donald Trump would have won by 21 points. “I was campaigning in communities that were over 60% rural, white, Southern, and we came within one point,” said Pearson, who is Black. “It is possible to win here.” His narrow defeat — and Democratic optimism — is part of a pattern that has repeated across the Deep South up and down the midterm ballot, where the blue wave that engulfed other parts of the country only lapped at Alabama, Louisiana, Mississippi and Tennessee. In these states, Republicans held onto power, for the most part. But Democrats made significant inroads that would have seemed unthinkable a year ago: from a nail-biting Senate race in Mississippi where the Democrat squeaked out a win over the Republican incumbent to down-ballot races where Democrats flipped state legislative seats in areas where Trump won with wide margins just two years ago. “You knock enough doors, you talk to enough people, you go to enough places, and you’re hearing the same stories,” said Pearson. “Republicans who say, ‘You’re the first Democrat I’ve ever voted for,’ and people who’ve never voted in their lives saying, ‘I’m registering to vote to vote for you because I want something different.’” But how durable are those gains? In a region full of Republican legislative supermajorities, where Trump remains popular and where few Democrats have held statewide offices in more than a decade, do the midterm results signal a change in the South’s political future, or were they an anomaly driven by a unique set of circumstances? Many experts remain skeptical that states such as Alabama or Mississippi are on a path to become neighboring Georgia, which is now a solid battleground state where Democrats won every statewide seat on the ballot this year. They see midterm results as not an embrace of Democrats so much as a negative referendum on Trump. “I know Democrats get excited in places like Alabama and Louisiana and Mississippi when Democrats win elections,” said David Hughes, a political science associate professor at the University of Louisiana at Lafayette who studies the politics of the American South. Voters were primarily motivated by anger over issues including high costs, the Iran war and congressional redistricting, he said. “It’s interesting, but it’s largely a fluke and there will be a reversion to the mean.” But Southern Democrats see glimmers of opportunity for lasting, even generational change in wins such as Democrat Scott Colom’s in Mississippi, where he beat Republican incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith on a razor-thin margin to become the first Black senator from the state since Reconstruction. Or in U.S. Rep. Shomari Figures, who defeated his Republican opponent in an Alabama congressional district that state legislators redrew this year to favor Republicans. And they see it in surprisingly close gubernatorial races in Tennessee and Florida, where Republicans eked out wins with one or two percentage points over their Democratic opponents. None of that means the Deep South has suddenly become a different place politically, said Anneshia Hardy, a voting rights activist in Alabama who studies Southern politics. “But it does mean that we need to pay closer attention to what’s happening beneath the statewide results,” she said. “The political landscape is not nearly as static as our electoral map suggests.” On a national level, she said, Democrats could learn from the South about building coalitions and creating political opportunities where they don’t already hold power. Quoting Andre 3000, the famed Atlanta rapper and half of hip-hop duo Outkast, she said, “‘The South got something to say,’ and I hope folks are listening.” Voting rights and Black political power In a region that was the epicenter of the fight for voting rights 60 years ago, the recent congressional redistricting ignited a fire among voters, and particularly among Black voters, who showed up to the polls in numbers rarely seen in a midterm election, activists and experts told Stateline. The U.S. Supreme Court’s decision in Louisiana v. Callais earlier this year all but nullified a provision in the federal 1965 Voting Rights Act that required states to draw electoral maps to give racial minority voters the opportunity to elect their chosen candidates. Republican state legislators rushed to redraw their congressional maps to favor GOP candidates in Alabama, Florida, Louisiana, North Carolina, Tennessee and Texas. Democrats tried gerrymandering in California and Virginia. That redistricting decision was pivotal for Southern voters, and for Black voters in particular, Pearson said. “I think if that had not happened, we would not have seen a number of the victories we saw,” he said. “To have such an ignited and excited Black Democratic voting base, I think the attack on voting rights was the key issue that really awakened people’s attentiveness and conscientiousness.” Midterm turnout is typically much lower than it is for presidential elections. But this year saw historic turnout, even in the South. Democrats saw their share of the vote increase in every county in states such as Alabama, where Democratic turnout nearly doubled over 2022 numbers while GOP votes declined slightly. Nearly 1 million Mississippians turned out to vote, rivaling presidential election years. One-third of Mississippi and Louisiana ballots were cast by Black voters. In Georgia, turnout among Black voters increased more than 11% over the 2022 midterms while white turnout shrank. Activists say the high turnout in the South was built on decades of voter outreach and community organizing, particularly in Black communities. It just needed a spark to ignite, they said. Republicans lit the match when they began gerrymandering in earnest earlier this year. The newly drawn maps provided a tangible example for casual voters to see how state and national leaders wield power, and how they can take it away from their constituents, Hardy said. Louisiana, the state at the center of the Supreme Court’s Callais case, saw voter turnout surge especially in parishes — the state’s equivalent of counties — where congressional lines were redrawn, said Louisiana political consultant Mary-Patricia Wray, who’s worked on statewide campaigns for both Republicans and Democrats. “Voters are very much aware that when we elect our legislature, it will be in charge of redrawing our maps again,” Wray said. “I think that awareness truly did drive Black turnout in Louisiana specifically, and I think it did in any state where there was a potential to have an impact on congressional maps.” Democrats nationally had their best performance with white voters in years, tying with Republicans for white voters after not having won white voters in a presidential election since 1964. In the growing urban center of Madison County, Alabama, a majority-white electorate flipped three state house seats from red to blue, and sent down-ballot Republican incumbents packing, including the incumbent sheriff. In suburban, majority-white Rutherford County south of Nashville, Tennessee, Democrats flipped three state House seats. “One of the surprising things about Democrats doing well in the South was that many of these weren’t on the radar” of the national Democratic party, “and they won anyway, with little resources,” said Kent Syler, a political science professor at Middle Tennessee State University. “Now they’ve demonstrated that there’s an opportunity here, you’re going to see more recruitment of top-quality candidates and you’re going to see more resources for those candidates, because this election proved you have a chance.” Looking ahead Louisiana and Mississippi are two of just three states — Kentucky is the other — that will hold elections for state offices and legislative seats in 2027. And Democratic near-misses in those states are already fueling speculation over the next round of elections. Democrat Jamie Davis, who lost the Senate race in Louisiana to Republican U.S. Rep. Julia Letlow by about 25,000 votes, less than a two-point margin, is reportedly eyeing a run for governor. But the political climate remains volatile. “Neither party can take anything for granted. The electorate is just ticked off,” said Hughes, of the University of Louisiana at Lafayette. “If Democrats don’t find a way to deliver (on their promises), I have confidence that the voters will turn them out of office down the line.” One thing the South showed national Democrats as well as Republicans, several experts told Stateline, was that more moderate candidates who avoided national disagreements over wedge issues tended to do better at the polls. “I saw a preference for moderate incumbents over extreme incumbents at every level of the ballot,” for both parties, said Wray, the Louisiana political consultant. Hughes thinks it will take a greater demographic shift — voters moving in from other states and bringing their politics with them, plus a continued rise in turnout from Black voters and other minority groups — to create the conditions in states such as Alabama that propelled Georgia or North Carolina to swing-state status. Democrats across the South are hoping for more investment from national groups, now that the South has shown a win is possible. They’re looking at the tens of millions poured into races in Texas and Georgia, arguing even a fraction of that could make a difference in state houses and governor’s mansions across the region — and from there, influence political control of the nation’s highest offices. Pearson said he’s working on creating a political action committee to continue building on the Democratic successes and near-successes of the midterms. “I believe the litmus test for America’s democracy is what happens in the South,” he said. “We can perfect this American experiment if we invest in the South and I’m more hopeful and optimistic about us doing it than ever before.” Stateline reporter Anna Claire Vollers can be reached at avollers@stateline.org. A California billionaire tax proposal faced a major setback despite big wins for progressives
articles.description: A California billionaire tax proposal faced a major setback despite big wins for progressives AP News What a wealth tax looks like in the age of AI billionaires CNN California nixed a billionaire tax. In WA, voters want to soak the rich The Seattle Times Opinion | Government Gets a Tax Windfall From Anthropic WSJ California entrepreneur says state avoided economic disaster with billionaire tax rejection Fox Business
articles.content: SACRAMENTO, Calif. (AP) — In an election with major wins for Democrats and progressives nationwide, California voters not only rejected the biggest test yet for a state wealth tax, they also approved a measure making it much harder to enact one in the future. Proposition 40 would have imposed a one-time 5% tax on the wealth of Californians whose net worth exceeds $1 billion, with most of the money dedicated to healthcare. Just more than half — 52% — of voters rejected it. Meanwhile, they narrowly approved Proposition 42, which bans the state from enacting future taxes on people’s financial assets. State lawmakers can’t override that; it can only be undone by voters with a future ballot measure. “I don’t think you’re going to see such a good Democratic electorate in the near future,” said Wesley Hussey, a political science professor at California State University, Sacramento. “This was the time to pass something that was pretty lefty and progressive and had a lot of opposition.” Nationally it was a good year for so-called “tax the rich” measures in other states, including Washington, where voters upheld a 9.9% tax on household income over $1 million. But California’s measure was different because it would have taxed the assets, not the income, of the ultrarich. And it targeted billionaires, who are significantly wealthier than millionaires and have far more assets to spend. A committee that opposed Proposition 40 and backed Proposition 42 raised more than $333 million, including large donations from tech billionaires such as Google co-founder Sergey Brin and former Google CEO Eric Schmidt. Collectively, the fight over taxing billionaires was one of the most expensive ballot battles in state history. Outside observers say the fact that it failed in California, a heavily Democratic state often viewed as a liberal leader, is not surprising because of the sheer amount of money spent opposing it and the big-name Democrats who lined up against it. Gov. Gavin Newsom was among those warning it was a bad financial deal for the state. Opponents outspent supporters by 10 to 1. But proponents of the wealth tax, which included SEIU United Healthcare Workers West, U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders and U.S. Rep. Ro Khanna, are trying to frame the loss as progress toward holding billionaires accountable in the future. They have teased bringing the idea before voters again in 2028. “The game is up, people have had it and this election is just the beginning,” Khanna said on election night. Faced with pushback from Newsom, SEIU UHW offered to scale back its proposal in June just before it qualified for the ballot. The union proposed a 2% levy, down from 5%, but Newsom’s office said the proposed tax remained fundamentally flawed. Efforts to make a deal fell apart, and the union proceeded despite a growing coalition of groups opposing the tax. Opponents of the tax said its failure affirmed that voters understood the risks associated with it. They warned it would have driven billionaires and their tax money out of state, causing budget problems down the road. California relies heavily on the rich for its income tax revenue. “We were hopefully optimistic based on the polls that voters would agree with us that Prop. 40 was just a horrible idea for the state and Prop. 42 provides some important protections going forward,” said David Kline, a spokesperson for the California Taxpayers Association. California voters didn’t completely repudiate the concept of taxing the wealthy at higher rates in this year’s election. They approved a measure to indefinitely extend a tax increase on individual incomes exceeding $371,000 to raise money for education. Besides Washington, Colorado voters adopted a graduated income tax that imposes higher rates on people with higher income, including an 8.4% tax on income over $1 million. The revenue from both states’ taxes will go toward education, healthcare and other services. Spending on the Washington and Colorado measures paled in comparison to the billionaire tax battle. Legislatures in Hawaii, Maine and Rhode Island also approved new taxes this year on people with incomes over $1 million. California has a 1% income tax on millionaires that voters approved in 2004 to raise money for mental health services. Carl Davis, research director at the nonprofit Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy, said the results indicated “a really good batting average” for backers of higher taxes for the wealthy. California’s billionaire tax effort was hurt by divisions among organized labor over the measure, he said. “I think the pendulum is swinging toward increased interest in taxing the rich,” he said. Advocates for higher taxes on the wealthy plan to expand their push next year in a half-dozen states where Democrats recently won control of both legislative chambers and the governor’s office, said Amber Wallin, executive director of the State Revenue Alliance, a nonprofit advocacy group for progressive tax policies. “I think that the movement will only continue to grow,” Wallin said. California’s Proposition 42 bans new taxes on people’s financial assets, business interests and intellectual property, as well as taxes that apply retroactively. The billionaire tax, for instance, would have applied to people living in the state as of Jan. 1, 2026, even though it would have taken effect the following year. That will now be prohibited. California Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra, a Democrat who will take over from Newsom in January, opposed the billionaire tax. But he said recently that the amount of support it received sent “a clear signal” that people “don’t believe everybody in California is paying their fair share.” He said he wanted to correct that but didn’t specify how. Lorena Gonzalez, president of the California Federation of Labor Unions, which supported Proposition 40, said opposition from groups like the California Teachers Association and Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California made it harder to pass the measure than if supporters had been fighting billionaires alone. But she said this year’s ballot fight was just the start. “We have to go back to the ballot,” Gonzalez said. “We’ve got to keep fighting.” Associated Press writer David A. Lieb in Jefferson City, Missouri, contributed.

In Ukraine, the fight to keep winter outside begins with a broken window
articles.description: In Ukraine, the fight to keep winter outside begins with a broken window AP News A $438,000 bet on Kyiv — Why open a restaurant ahead of a winter of blackouts? The Kyiv Independent Kyiv's restaurant owners brace for tough winter as war pressures mount Reuters How one Ukrainian family gets ready for another winter at war NPR Russian attacks on Ukraine's energy grid intensify ahead of winter ABC News - Breaking News, L
articles.content: KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — For weeks after a missile exploded in front of her apartment block, Oleksandra Horban found pieces of glass in her small apartment. She threw out her 2-year-old son’s plush toys which were covered with glass shards. Outside her ground-floor home, mangled window frames were piled onto a mountain of debris awaiting removal. Pieces of glass were mixed with autumn leaves on the muddy ground. “Even now we still find glass,” Horban said. “If we vacuum three times, wash the floor and clean up, we’ll still find those microscopic pieces somewhere, in the bed or in the toys.” As winter sets in, Ukraine is facing a severe shortage of replacement windows with Russian missile and drone attacks continuing to damage buildings, leaving residents exposed to the cold. Temperatures in Kyiv fell to minus 20 degrees Celsius (minus 4 degrees Fahrenheit) last winter. Windows are boarded up with wooden panels in an apartment building damaged in a Russian missile strike in Kyiv, Ukraine, Wednesday, Nov. 4, 2026. (AP Photo/Evgeniy Maloletka) Windows are boarded up with wooden panels in an apartment building damaged in a Russian missile strike in Kyiv, Ukraine, Wednesday, Nov. 4, 2026. (AP Photo/Evgeniy Maloletka) Government assistance can take months, skilled installers are in short supply and replacement costs have soared, hitting low-income districts near industrial zones hardest. Horban lives in a Soviet-era “groundscraper” — an enormous horizontal apartment block in the Ukrainian capital. A missile blast in October damaged a vertical section of apartments and shattered hundreds of facade windows. Most shattered windows have been temporarily covered with fiberboard or tarps. Some boards have small openings fitted with Plexiglas to let daylight into apartments. New windows in Horban’s apartment would cost about $1,700, more than three times the country’s average salary. Government compensation can take three to four months. A worker installs a new window at an apartment building damaged in a Russian missile strike in Kyiv, Ukraine, Wednesday, Nov. 4, 2026. (AP Photo/Evgeniy Maloletka) A worker installs a new window at an apartment building damaged in a Russian missile strike in Kyiv, Ukraine, Wednesday, Nov. 4, 2026. (AP Photo/Evgeniy Maloletka) Many cannot afford to wait. Without proper windows, apartments are exposed to cold, damp and mold, particularly during power outages. Housing damage is among the largest costs of the war. An estimated 3 million housing units were destroyed or badly damaged by the end of last year, adding $90 billion to Ukraine’s reconstruction needs, according to the World Bank. Ukraine’s window manufacturers can meet demand for replacement windows. The bottleneck is the shortage of skilled installers. Mykhailo Orlenko, executive director of the Association of Ukrainian Manufacturers of Transparent Structures, said businesses were unable to exempt their employees from military service, including many installers. “The market lost a large number of these specialists,” he said. Factories can manufacture windows in about 10 working days, but installation can be delayed for a lot longer as customers wait for a crew to become available. High demand means installation bills have at least doubled over the past year. Oleksandr, a 42-year-old installer who has worked in the industry for 25 years, said power outages add to the challenges. His team relies on battery-powered tools and normally has to carry heavy materials up stairs with elevators out of service. On one recent job, his team replaced balcony doors and windows in a fourth-floor apartment, carrying the materials up by hand. A worker installs a new window at an apartment building damaged in a Russian missile strike in Kyiv, Ukraine, Wednesday, Nov. 4, 2026. (AP Photo/Evgeniy Maloletka) A worker installs a new window at an apartment building damaged in a Russian missile strike in Kyiv, Ukraine, Wednesday, Nov. 4, 2026. (AP Photo/Evgeniy Maloletka) “That was 18 trips up and down the stairs, carrying heavy loads. It would have been easier with a working elevator, but we didn’t wait for the power to come back on — we got straight to work,” he said. Oleksandr asked to be identified only by his first name, citing security concerns following Russian attacks on private businesses. To address the shortage, the industry is investing in training. A vocational college in Kyiv opened a European Union-funded facility in March, where 26 10th graders have started a three-year program to become window, door and facade installers. Teenagers in new overalls practice around mock window openings built from brick, cinder block, wood and synthetic materials. Their classes are frequently disrupted by missile and drone alerts. The program was established after professional associations lobbied the government to formally recognize window installation as a profession, allowing the industry to access grants and create structured training courses. Mykhailo Orlenko, executive director of the Association of Ukrainian Manufacturers of Transparent Structures, explains to students window construction at a technical college in Kyiv, Ukraine, Wednesday, Nov. 4, 2026. (AP Photo/Evgeniy Maloletka) Mykhailo Orlenko, executive director of the Association of Ukrainian Manufacturers of Transparent Structures, explains to students window construction at a technical college in Kyiv, Ukraine, Wednesday, Nov. 4, 2026. (AP Photo/Evgeniy Maloletka) Graduates can expect starting salaries of around $900, on par with those of law graduates due to Ukraine’s acute skill drain, Orlenko said. Instructor Volodymyr Tserbii hopes the apprentices will help rebuild the country, their training offering students a path into a profession needed for reconstruction. The massive task of repairing Ukraine’s damaged homes, schools, roads, power plants and other infrastructure will take at least a decade, according to government planners. For Horban, the wait for new windows is added to a long list of her household’s problems. Her apartment has no gas, forcing the family to cook on a portable cylinder. They heat their son’s room when electricity is available. A leaking kitchen roof has added to the damage. The blast also left her toddler son, Viacheslav, frightened. The sounds of war have become part of his vocabulary. Pressing his nose against a windowpane that survived the attack, he waves to passersby and asks his mother whether more bombing is coming, using the words “bam bam” to describe the explosions. “This is not life, this is surviving,” Horban said. “This is dragging out an existence, not a life.” Vasilisa Stepanenko, Evgeniy Maloletka and Susie Blann in Kyiv contributed.
